name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
1. At eighteen, applying for my first job, I remember thinking very clearly: not sales. Anything but sales.

I ended up spending the better part of the next twelve years in roles that were, if I'm honest with myself, sales wearing a different job title. Executive assistant to a CEO, coordinating deals I told myself I was just "supporting." Business development. Marketing that somehow always circled back to closing something.

I used to tell people, half joking, that sales just wasn't my thing and I'd rather find something else entirely. I believed it for a long time.

What changed wasn't that I suddenly became a closer. I'm still not, and I've made peace with that. What changed is I noticed the thing I kept avoiding was also the thing I was quietly good at every time I got close enough to it: not pitching hard, just being useful to someone until trust built on its own.

Turns out that's most of what this job is. I just needed twelve years and a title with "Account Executive" in it to admit that the thing I ran from was already my thing the whole time.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
2. A prospect ghosted our onboarding three separate times. Not rude about it, just quiet. Kept meaning to, kept not getting to it.

Then last month, unprompted: "didn't expect to still be using this three months in, but here we are."

I didn't do anything clever to make that happen. I just didn't stop showing up. A casual check-in here, a genuine "hey, this update might solve the thing you mentioned" there, never with any edge to it, never making someone feel bad about going quiet the last three times.

I learned this the slow way, years ago, working with agencies where a twelve month sales cycle was completely normal and nobody blinked at it. You stop expecting the yes to arrive on your timeline. You just keep the door open and mean it every time.

Most sales advice is built around the pitch. Mine is built around what happens for the eleven months after the pitch, when nothing's happening on the surface and you're the only one still paying attention.

The close isn't the moment. It's whatever you did in all the quiet months before it that made someone comfortable enough to come back on their own.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
3. I have a low hum of needing to be doing something useful, even when there's nothing urgent happening. A friend once called it main character productivity guilt. Close enough.

The thing that quiets it fastest isn't a productivity system. It's just moving somewhere else. A different café, a different corner of the apartment, once memorably a co-working space with a chair considerably less comfortable than my actual desk chair.

Something about a new environment resets whatever loop is running. I don't fully understand the mechanism. I just know that when I'm stuck, staring at the same wall I've been staring at for three hours, the fix is almost never "push through." It's leave.

I used to feel a little embarrassed admitting that changing my scenery does more for my output than any calendar blocking technique I've tried. It felt like a soft answer to a problem I thought needed a disciplined one.

It's not soft. It's just the actual lever, for me specifically, and I've stopped pretending I should need a more impressive-sounding one.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
4. Eight years ago I was an executive assistant. Today I build the operating systems that let AI companies scale revenue without their delivery quietly falling apart underneath them.

Nobody plans that specific path. It just accumulated, one operational fire at a time.

As an EA, I ended up owning a CRM migration nobody else wanted to touch, because "just handle it" turned out to include the parts everyone else was avoiding. That migration contributed to a 2.5x revenue year, not because I closed anything myself, but because sales stopped losing deals to bad data.

Years later, running marketing operations at a dev shop, we actually doubled our profit target in a single year by fixing the boring stuff: the handoffs between sales and delivery, the pricing logic nobody had revisited since the company was three people.

Most recently, automating close to 70% of client onboarding at an AI automation company, while revenue tripled around it.

None of these were the exciting part of anyone's job description. I've built an entire career out of being the person who goes and fixes the unglamorous connective tissue between departments, the part everyone agrees is a problem and nobody wants to own.

Turns out that's a valuable thing to be good at.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
5. Writing has never come easily to me. Neither has being consistent about much of anything creative. I've started, stopped, and quietly abandoned more content plans than I'd like to count.

What I've always had instead is a stubborn refusal to just stop doing something because I'm bad at it.

At eighteen I was convinced sales wasn't my thing. Spent the next decade proving myself wrong by accident, one sales-adjacent job at a time. Karaoke is the same story on a smaller, sillier scale, not a good singer, and somehow that fact has never once stopped me from getting up there.

There's a version of "find your strengths and only do those" that's quietly bad advice. It sounds efficient. What it does is let you avoid the exact things that would eventually become strengths, if you'd just kept doing them badly for long enough to get less bad.

I'm not trying to become a great writer. I'm trying to find whatever version of showing up and saying something real turns out to be mine, the same way I eventually found that in sales despite spending years insisting it wasn't for me.

The skill was never the point. The not-quitting was.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
6. Wrote our August product update this week, and looking back at the list, none of it is flashy. All of it is stuff people asked for.

Instagram Reels now works the same way YouTube Shorts already did: point at one long video, get a week of native clips with subtitles and descriptions already written. Carousels jumped to 20 images. Small thing, kept coming up.

The one I'm personally most into: you can now highlight just the line in a post that isn't landing and regenerate only that part. Before, a weak opening meant rerolling the entire post and losing copy you'd already liked. That always bugged me more than it probably should have.

Link placement is now per platform too. Leave it in-post on X, drop it to the first comment on LinkedIn, because that's how each platform treats it.

None of this is a headline feature. It's the unglamorous stuff that determines whether you keep using a tool six weeks in or quietly drift back to doing it manually. Every one of these came from someone telling us exactly where it slowed them down.

If something in your own workflow still takes longer than it should, that's still the fastest way onto our roadmap. Just tell us.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
7. The best advice in our own automation guide isn't about which tool to use. It's a line about building a kill switch.

Pause all your scheduled content automatically during a natural disaster, a national tragedy, a PR mess, anything where posting on autopilot reads as tone-deaf. Most brands find out they needed one the exact week they didn't have it.

The other one that stuck with me: don't fully automate everything, especially your one or two main platforms. An 80/20 split, mostly automated, a real slice still written and posted by an actual human in the moment, tends to hold up a lot better than either extreme.

And stagger your post times. If your best window is 9 to 10am, don't schedule for 9:00 sharp. Something like 9:28 reads as a person who happened to post then, not a queue firing on the hour.

None of these are secrets. They're just the specific, slightly boring discipline that separates a brand that automates well from one that automates and then gets quietly weird the one week it mattered to sound human.

Automation is supposed to buy you the judgment calls back. Not remove them.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
8. Before any of my actual job titles, I co-founded a volunteer group in Minsk called Prodobro. Over about three years we ran more than seventy events for two family-based orphanages and a neurological center, coordinating volunteers, doing the PR, chasing the funding, all of it with basically no budget and a lot of stubbornness.

Nobody teaches you operations in a context like that. You learn it because a volunteer cancels the morning of an event and forty kids are still showing up regardless of what your schedule said.

What I carry from those three years into corporate work now isn't a specific skill. It's a baseline for what "urgent" means. A client Slack message at 9pm is not urgent. A broken pipeline connecting a CRM to a paid ad platform is not urgent. I learned the real version of urgent a long time before I ever touched a CRM.

That baseline has been quietly useful for a decade. It's hard to panic convincingly about a missed deadline in enterprise software once you've run an event for kids who don't have much else going for them that week, with two volunteers who no-showed and a donated van that didn't arrive.

Everything since has felt, structurally, a little more solvable than it probably should.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
9. My work has spanned SaaS, AI, software development, tobacco of all things during an early internship. Health tech is the one industry I keep finding a reason to come back to, even when nothing about my actual role requires it.

I can't fully explain why, but I've noticed the pattern enough times now to trust it. At a health tech global summit in Basel, walking a floor full of people building tools for hospitals and clinics, I felt a genuinely specific kind of attention I don't feel the same way at a general SaaS conference. Not more professional interest. Something closer to caring whether the thing being pitched works.

Most of my actual career has been industry-agnostic by design, operations and revenue systems apply the same underlying logic whether you're selling automation to restaurants or workflow software to enterprise. That's been a genuine strength professionally.

Health tech is the one place that logic still applies and the stakes underneath it feel different anyway. A broken onboarding flow for a marketing tool is an inconvenience. A broken workflow for a clinical team is a different category of problem entirely.

I don't know yet what I'll do with that soft spot. I just know it's real, and I've stopped pretending it's the same as my interest in everything else I've worked on.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
10. Three years running revenue operations at a dev shop, closing and managing long-term contracts with companies like Wagepoint, HolacracyOne, Dealmaker, and SpendHound. None of those are household names. All of them taught me something specific about selling technical delivery to technical buyers.

A software agency selling engineering time to other software companies has a harder sales problem than most people assume. Your buyer has almost certainly evaluated a dozen agencies before you, they can smell a padded estimate from the first call, and "we're really passionate about your mission" gets you nowhere with someone who's shipped code themselves.

What worked was radical specificity in scoping. Not a vague statement of work. An actual breakdown of what gets built, in what order, with what's explicitly out of scope stated as clearly as what's in it. Technical buyers trust precision more than enthusiasm.

We also coordinated a Product Hunt launch for an internal product that hit the Top 10 that day, which taught me a completely different lesson: a launch you've planned for weeks still lives or dies in about six real-time hours, and having a team ready to respond to comments in that window matters more than the weeks of prep leading up to it.

Different skill, same underlying instinct. Show up specific, show up ready, and don't let the moment that matters catch you unprepared.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
11. I recommend people rarely, and specifically. When I do, it's almost never because of their resume line items.

The thing I'm watching for, across a decade of working alongside people in sales-adjacent and operations roles, is energy that survives a boring task. Anyone can be engaged during a pitch or a big launch. The real signal is whether someone stays sharp and cares during the unglamorous stretch, the fortieth support ticket of the week, the CRM cleanup nobody wants to own, the reporting nobody reads until suddenly everyone does.

I've watched candidates interview brilliantly and then visibly deflate the moment a role's actual day-to-day got described. I've also watched people who undersold themselves in an interview turn out to be the ones still fully present three years later, still bringing real energy to tasks that stopped being interesting to anyone else in the room a long time ago.

That's rare, and it's the entire reason I'll go out of my way to recommend someone publicly when I see it, rather than treating a recommendation as a formality you owe a former colleague.

Skills are teachable. Whatever keeps someone's actual attention present during the boring forty percent of a job is not, and it's the only thing I trust when I'm the one putting my name behind someone.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
12. [new] Distribution.Ai didn't start as a product. It started as a problem Ross kept hitting running Foundation, his content agency, over and over, with almost every single client.

The content itself was never the bottleneck. Teams could write a great blog post, record a solid podcast episode, produce a useful video. What broke, every time, was what happened after publish. One piece of content, one platform, one post, and then it just sat there. Getting it properly reshaped for five different platforms every single week meant someone manually rewriting the same idea five separate times, forever, which is exactly the kind of task that quietly never gets done consistently no matter how much everyone agrees it should.

So the team built the thing they needed internally first. Not a scheduling tool. A system that took one real asset and turned it into platform-native versions across all of it, in your own voice, without you rewriting the same paragraph five times in five different boxes.

It worked well enough internally that it became obvious it wasn't just a Foundation problem. It was everyone's problem who'd ever hit publish once and watched the effort behind that piece of content stop paying the moment the initial wave of attention passed.

That's the whole origin story. Not a big vision. A specific, recurring pain nobody had fixed properly yet.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
13. [new] Something's shifted in the last few months that most people posting content still haven't adjusted for: a meaningful share of your future buyers are no longer finding you through a feed at all. They're finding you, or not finding you, through an AI answer.

Someone asks ChatGPT or Perplexity a question your content answers well. If your content isn't structured and distributed in a way that shows up in that answer, it doesn't matter how good the original piece was. It's invisible to that entire research moment.

I've started treating this as a genuine, separate distribution channel now, not a hypothetical future thing. Content that gets repurposed and spread across multiple platforms, in slightly different framings each time, shows up in more of the source material these answer engines are pulling from. A single blog post living only on your own site is a much smaller footprint than the same idea living natively across five platforms.

Most teams are still optimizing purely for the feed scroll. The ones who'll have an advantage in a year are the ones treating AI-answer visibility as its own real target now, while most of the market is still catching up to the fact that it's already happening.

This isn't a prediction. It's already showing up in how people reach us.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
14. [new] Save this one. Fifteen things to post about when you don't know what to post about.

A customer result you can share, even a small one.
A mistake you made and what you'd do differently.
A question a prospect asked that you didn't have a great answer for yet.
Something you changed your mind about this year.
A tool or workflow you rely on that nobody asked about.
The worst piece of advice you got early in your career.
A trend everyone's talking about, and your actual honest take on it.
Something a customer said that you're still thinking about.
A decision you almost made and didn't.
What your first ninety days at your current company looked like.
A person you'd recommend without hesitation, and why.
The most boring part of your job that turns out to matter the most.
A number from your own work you're either proud of or still chasing.
Something you believed a year ago that turned out wrong.
The one question you wish more people asked you.

Pick one. Write four sentences about it. That's the whole bar for a post that's worth someone's ten seconds.

Bookmark this for the next time you're staring at a blank compose box.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
15. [new] Everything we've shipped in the last 90 days, in one place, because I keep forgetting how much landed once I stop and list it out.

Long videos now auto-cut into YouTube Shorts, subtitled and described automatically.
That same cutting now publishes natively to Instagram Reels too, not just YouTube.
Carousels jumped from a small image cap to 20 images per post.
An AI chat now lives inside the product, and you can highlight just the line that isn't working and regenerate only that part, instead of rerolling an entire post you mostly liked.
Link placement is now controlled per platform. In-post on X, first comment on LinkedIn, whatever each platform rewards.
Style Preferences now takes written custom instructions and file uploads, so the rules that don't fit into a toggle finally have somewhere to live.
The posting queue got a faster, more editable interface, time slots adjustable right in the table.

None of these individually is a headline feature. Stacked together over one quarter, it's a different product than the one we had in June.

The pattern behind all of it is the same: one piece of content should keep working long after publish day, across every platform, without you manually rebuilding it each time.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
16. [new] I use Distribution.Ai on my own content, which sounds like an obvious thing for someone selling it to say, but I want to show the math instead of just claiming it.

A few months ago my posting was inconsistent at best, the classic pattern, a burst of three posts in a good week and then two weeks of nothing while I told myself I'd get to it. I started running my own drafts, voice memos, half-formed thoughts I'd normally never turn into anything, through our own repurposing flow instead.

The difference wasn't that AI suddenly made me a better writer. It's that the actual blank-page moment disappeared. I'd have a rough first version to react to and edit, instead of a cursor blinking on nothing, which turned out to be the actual thing stopping me, not a lack of ideas.

Going from a following that barely moved for months to growing again wasn't one viral post. It was just removing the friction that kept me from posting consistently enough for anything to compound in the first place.

I'm not a case study we wrote up for the website. I'm just the person who uses the product every single week because the alternative is going back to staring at a blank box, and I already know how that story ends.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
17. [new] You publish a great podcast episode. It gets attention for about four days. Then it's gone, buried under whatever published after it, and all the actual effort that went into it, the guest booking, the editing, the thinking, stops earning anything.

That's not a content problem. That's a distribution problem, and most teams never fix it because it feels like a smaller issue than it is.

Here's what extends a piece of content's working life:

Pull three to five distinct moments out of the full episode, not just one highlight, and treat each as its own post.
Rewrite the same core idea in a different framing for each platform, not the same caption pasted five places.
Space the repurposed pieces out over two to three weeks instead of publishing them all in the same week as the original.
Track which specific moment got engagement, then lean into more of that angle next time instead of guessing again from scratch.
Let one strong repurposed post become a standalone topic for a future piece of long-form content, so the cycle feeds itself.

The podcast episode isn't the asset. The five or six ideas buried inside it are, and most of them never get pulled out at all.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
18. [new] A few years ago, running marketing operations at a dev shop, we nearly lost a client relationship worth a meaningful share of that year's revenue over a scoping mistake that was entirely avoidable, and entirely ours.

A project budget had been estimated against an old pricing model nobody had updated in months. By the time the mismatch surfaced, we were already deep into delivery, the client was expecting a scope we could no longer profitably deliver at the agreed price, and the honest conversation ahead of us was the kind that ends relationships.

I remember sitting with the numbers the night before that call, unsure whether we'd still have this client by the end of the week.

What saved it wasn't a clever negotiation. It was walking in and explaining exactly what went wrong, on our side, with no spin, and proposing a specific fix that cost us real margin that quarter. No blame redirected, no vague reassurance, just the actual mistake and the actual plan to make it right.

The client stayed. Longer than that one project, as it turned out.

That mismatch is the entire reason I've been borderline obsessive about pricing logic and margin alignment in every operations role since. I'd rather build the boring safeguard now than have that conversation again.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
18. I speak four languages. Belarusian first, then Russian, English, and enough Polish to get through a client call without switching to English halfway.

Nobody's ever hired me specifically for that. It shows up in a quieter way instead.

Working across North American and European markets for most of my career, I've noticed something that doesn't get talked about much: the actual sales objection sounds different depending on which market you're in, even when the underlying concern is identical. A US prospect will say the price feels high. A prospect somewhere in Central Europe will more often ask what happens if it doesn't work, framing the same hesitation as risk instead of cost.

(1) I catch that distinction faster than someone working purely in one market would, because I've had to translate the same concern across enough languages and enough cultural registers to notice the pattern underneath the specific words.

(2) It's also made me suspicious of sales scripts written for one market and quietly rolled out everywhere. The words translate. The actual hesitation being addressed often doesn't map cleanly at all.

I don't lead with the languages on my profile. I probably should. It's done more for how I sell than half the certifications sitting above it.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
19. Being a Founding AE means there's no playbook to inherit. You're the one writing it, in real time, while also carrying quota.

Nobody warns you how disorienting that is in the first few weeks. Every other sales role I've had came with a script, an objection-handling doc, a deck someone before me had already tested against real prospects. This one came with a product and a calendar.

What I've learned building this from zero: the instinct to wait until you're fully confident before running a call is the wrong instinct. You run the call slightly under-prepared, you write down exactly what worked and what didn't the moment it's over, and by call twenty you have a real playbook that nobody handed you, built from actual objections instead of guessed ones.

The version of the pitch I use now barely resembles the one I opened with in month one. Not because the product changed. Because month one me was still answering questions prospects weren't asking, and it took real conversations to figure out which ones they were.

I'd rather be five months into building something true than five months into reciting something borrowed that never quite fit.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
20. I got certified in partner sales training this year, and one idea from it has quietly changed how I run every deal since: a partner referral isn't a warmer lead, it's a different sales process entirely.

Most reps treat a partner-sourced lead the same way they'd treat any inbound. Same pitch, same qualifying questions, just with a slightly friendlier opener because someone vouched for you.

That's leaving real advantage on the table.

A lead that came through a partner already has a layer of trust attached that a cold or even warm inbound lead doesn't. The prospect isn't evaluating whether to trust a stranger. They're evaluating whether the specific thing their trusted partner recommended is right for them.

That changes the entire first call. Less time proving credibility, more time confirming fit. Skip the parts of your usual pitch built to establish trust from zero, because that trust already exists, and spend the time you just freed up understanding their specific situation instead.

Reps who run partner leads through their standard playbook usually convert them fine. Reps who treat it as a different process convert them meaningfully better, and it's a small enough shift that almost nobody bothers making it.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
21. There has been much written about the buyer journey shortening, but I think the more useful question is where along that journey a buyer meets you first, and whether your company has any say in the matter.

Recent data shows that the majority of B2B buyers now form a meaningful view of a vendor before a sales conversation ever begins, and increasingly that view is shaped not by a single touchpoint but by a scattered, unpredictable set of them: a LinkedIn post read on a commute, a podcast clip surfaced by an algorithm, a summary an AI assistant generated on their behalf while researching a category they barely understood a week earlier. The buyer is not moving through a funnel in any tidy sense. They are assembling an impression from fragments, most of which the vendor never chose and often does not even know occurred.

This creates a genuine problem for companies who still plan content as a single asset published to a single channel. A blog post that lives only on your own site, however well researched, reaches a buyer who happens to search the exact right term at the exact right moment. Everyone else building the same impression through other channels, other formats, other algorithms, never encounters it at all.

I see two distinct failures in how companies typically respond to this.

The first is treating distribution as an afterthought, something a junior marketer manually handles after the real work of creation is finished, which in practice means it happens inconsistently or not at all once deadlines tighten.

The second is treating every channel identically, posting the same asset everywhere in the same form, which mistakes presence for relevance. A buyer encountering a native, platform-appropriate version of your thinking trusts it considerably more than one who recognizes a copy-pasted asset dropped somewhere it does not belong.

What works is treating a single piece of original thinking as raw material, not a finished output, and building genuine platform-native versions of it deliberately, at a cadence that keeps the same idea circulating across the fragments a buyer is assembling their impression from. This is not about producing more content. It is about respecting the reality that your buyer's journey through your brand happens on their terms, across surfaces you do not fully control, and your only genuine lever is making sure a well-considered version of your thinking is present wherever that assembly is happening.

Companies that treat distribution with the same rigour they apply to creation will build a materially stronger presence in a buyer's mind long before that buyer ever reaches out. The ones that do not will keep wondering why a good piece of content never seemed to move the number they were hoping it would.
